sources.cite: Python 3.15 documentation, struct: Interpret bytes as packed binary data
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch (page for Python 3.15.2): byte order '<' little-endian, '>' big-endian, '!' network (= big-endian); 'h' short and 'H' unsigned short, both standard size 2; unpack returns a tuple 'even if it contains exactly one item'. Two's complement: a 16-bit pattern with the top bit set is negative when read as signed, value minus 65,536 (the standard rule, worked in each reading's arithmetic: 0xF8C6 = 63,686, minus 65,536 = -1,850, so -18.50 °C).

Northbay Dairy, its gateways, frames, readings and deadline are invented teaching values; every decoded value follows from the bytes shown by the rules in the struct source. No real device is described.

brief.situation: You look after ingest.py at Northbay Dairy (fictional), which turns cold-store sensor frames into temperatures. Last night gateway G2 was replaced with a new model; since then its freezers read hundreds of degrees. The quality lead decides at 10:00 which pallets of ice cream ship. It is 09:05.
handover: The new gateway's notes say: temperature is a signed 16-bit integer, hundredths of a degree Celsius, little-endian.
Two handheld thermometer readings were taken at 07:30 on every freezer, as the cold-chain plan requires.
howItWorks: Pick a step from the action list: look at the raw bytes, read the notes, change the decoder, run a check, or send your answer. Nothing you pick is typed or executed: every step shows an authored result.
Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The deadline runs on the same clock.
The console shows the flags, the raw frames table, the decoder's code and the result of each step.
Sending your answer is final for this case. Afterwards you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the quality lead: why the readings were wrong, what you changed, and how you know the new ones are right.

parts.label: Why they were wrong
parts.criteria: Byte order and sign: the frame stores a 16-bit two's complement value least significant byte first; reading C6 F8 big-endian unsigned gives 0xC6F8 = 50,936 (509.36 °C); the right reading is 0xF8C6 = 63,686, top bit set, so 63,686 - 65,536 = -1,850 (-18.50 °C). Not faulty sensors.
parts.modelAnswer: Little-endian int16 read as big-endian uint16: both the byte order and the sign were wrong.

parts.label: What you changed
parts.criteria: The struct format becomes '<h'; swapping only the byte order or only the sign leaves the freezers wrong; dropping readings above 100 °C hides the real F3 excursion; the stored readings are not rewritten by a guess.
parts.modelAnswer: struct.unpack('<h', frame[4:6]); nothing filtered; stored data untouched.

parts.label: How you know
parts.criteria: Concordance with an independent measurement after the last change: the 07:30 handheld readings agree within 0.2 °C, which also confirms F3 really warmed.

scoring.modelReasoning: Impossible readings that appear with new hardware point to representation, not physics. The raw bytes for F1 are C6 F8. Read big-endian unsigned, 0xC6F8 is 50,936, so 509.36 °C. The notes say little-endian two's complement: least significant byte first gives 0xF8C6 = 63,686, and with the top bit set the signed value is 63,686 - 65,536 = -1,850, so -18.50 °C. Fixing only the byte order (636.86) or only the sign (-146.00) still fails. Struct format '<h' is both. Filtering readings above 100 °C would have hidden F3, really at -6.20 °C. Check against the independent handheld readings, then send.
